title: Controlling magnetic domain walls with supercurrents
authors: Tim Kokkeler, Risto Ojajärvi, F. Sebastian Bergeret, Tero T. Heikkilä
abstract: Establishing a versatile, fast and reliable magnetic memory technology is a giant bottleneck for cryogenic computing since present-day room-temperature solutions either cease to work or consume too much power. The long-term goal of superconducting spintronics has been to overcome this bottleneck by generating magnetic memories with equal-spin triplet supercurrent driven through them to control their magnetization direction. This path has been hampered by the short spin relaxation length and strong anisotropy in ferromagnets. Here we show how the supercurrent driven generation of spin accumulation in a superconductor/magnetic insulator bilayer, together with Gilbert damping of magnetization lead to a motion of magnetic domain walls. This manifests as a local voltage across the wall, which allows its position to be identified. Associated with this voltage and the current, there is Joule power which is dissipated via the Gilbert damping. The power required to maintain domain wall motion is orders of magnitude smaller than in the normal state, where most of the power is wasted in producing the current.
summary: This paper theoretically models the control of magnetic domain walls in superconductor/ferromagnetic insulator bilayers using supercurrents. It shows that the superconducting state allows for low-power, measurable motion of these walls by generating an equilibrium superfluid momentum. This work is significant for developing energy-efficient memory elements for cryogenic quantum computing applications.
main_problem: The research aims to develop a fast, reliable magnetic memory technology for cryogenic computing by controlling magnetic domain walls using superconducting supercurrents.
main_result: Supercurrent-driven motion of domain walls is predicted, generating a measurable voltage and dissipating power orders of magnitude lower than in normal state setups. The mechanism relies on the generation of an equilibrium superfluid momentum ($q_0$).
method: The analysis employs advanced theoretical techniques including quasiclassical Green's functions (Keldysh formalism), coupled action formulations for superconducting and magnetic systems, and solving coupled differential equations for domain wall dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a superconductor/ferromagnetic insulator bilayer. The physics involves coupling between supercurrent-induced spin accumulation (via ISGE) and the magnetization dynamics described by modified LLG equations.
key_observables: Domain wall velocity ($v_{dw}$), measurable voltage ($V \propto q_0 v_{dw}$), dissipated power ($P$), and temperature increase ($\Delta T$).
important_parameters: Supercurrent density ($j$), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), spin-orbit coupling strength, Gilbert damping parameter ($\alpha$), and the equilibrium superfluid momentum ($q_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes an adiabatic limit for motion (low speed) and that the FI is much thinner than the SC to ensure spin-charge coupling dominates over Oersted fields.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setup, domain wall dynamics under varying currents relative to a critical current ($I_W$), snapshots of superfluid momentum during motion, and theoretical derivations relating voltage/power to velocity.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the fundamental coupling mechanisms (ISGE, $q_0$ generation) to deriving the coupled equations of motion for domain wall coordinates. It then analyzes the resulting dynamics, power balance ($P=D$), and finally addresses thermal stability by calculating temperature increases due to dissipation.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed theoretical framework connecting superconducting phenomena (supercurrents, superfluid momentum) directly to spintronic memory elements (domain walls), offering insights into energy-efficient quantum/cryogenic device operation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Superconductor–ferromagnet bilayer. Magnetic proximity effect and SOC induce into the superconductor a helical superfluid momentum q0, whose sign changes across the domain wall. Supercurrent I induces an additional superfluid momentum qex. (b) Spin accumulation generated by the supercurrent via the spin-galvanic effect drives the domain wall (DW) at velocity vdw. Below the Walker breakdown current, I < IW, the wall moves with a fixed shape, while above the Walker breakdown current, I > IW, the spins in the domain wall precess while the wall moves. Figure 2. (a) Generation of equilibrium superfluid momentum by spin-galvanic effect. Magnetic proximity effect induces a Zeeman field in the SC (with direction m). Together with the polar vector n this generates a current, which is canceled by a superfluid momentum q0. (b) and (c) Generation of spin by supercurrent due to inverse spin galvanic effect (ISGE). The intrinsic ISGE generates an excess spin in the bulk of the SC due to broken inversion symmetry. The extrinsic ISGE (spin Hall effect) generates a transverse spin current which shows up as interfacial spin. Both mechanisms involve the polar vector n.

Figure 3. Electrical detection of the domain wall motion. (a) Setup with multiple voltage probes. (b) Sketch of the time-dependent voltage signal due to domain wall movement. The voltage is maximized when the domain wall is between the two probes. When the domain wall leaves, the signal decays sharply over a time-scale determined by the domain wall speed, and the domain wall size or the superconductor coherence length. After this initial period, a tail remains, which is exponentially suppressed in ∆ kBT , and extends over the charge imbalance relaxation time.

Spintronics.note: This paper directly models the physics in a superconductor/ferromagnetic insulator bilayer involving supercurrents and domain wall motion, fitting perfectly into the context of advanced spintronic heterostructures.
